What you will practice · Choose your pace

What you will practice

  • Clarify an executive mandate before selecting a growth option or commissioning broad analysis.
  • Make a strategic trade-off explicit when two attractive initiatives cannot both fit the available capacity.
  • Narrow a market-size claim and distinguish addressable spending, assumed capture, and available profit.
  • Explain a growing service's economics and challenge an unsupported claim that scale alone will solve the loss.
  • Compare competing investment requests on a consistent basis and expose displaced work and sunk-cost reasoning.

Choose your pace

Quick practice · 15 minutes: complete one short exchange, check the explanations, and read both roles aloud.

Extended practice · two or three sittings: check the case facts, study the vocabulary and phrases, complete the longer conversation, then rehearse the follow-up exchange.

Level guide: designed for intermediate to advanced learners. B1 learners can start with the short exchanges and supplied phrases; B2 learners can complete the cloze conversations; C1 learners can focus on the distinctions in the language checks. These are teaching suggestions, not a certified level assessment.

01Strategy Role, Problem Framing, and Executive DiagnosisGrowth is an ambition, not yet a clear assignment+

Your goal

Clarify an executive mandate before selecting a growth option or commissioning broad analysis.

This lesson in the book, page 4 ↗

A Read the situation

Growth is an ambition, not yet a clear assignment

Executive sponsor Daniel asks strategy lead Rina for a growth strategy. Last year the business reported $20 million revenue and $2 million operating profit. The sponsor has not chosen whether the primary objective is revenue growth, operating-profit improvement, or entry into a new market. No target, horizon, or spending limit has been agreed. A workshop is scheduled for Monday. Rina must establish the decision question and missing inputs rather than assume that an acquisition or a 20% revenue target has already been authorized.

Daniel: Executive sponsor / Rina: Strategy lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the primary unresolved issue?

Answer and explanation

C. Which outcome the growth strategy should prioritize

The sponsor has not chosen the main objective, so the analysis cannot assume a specific outcome or solution.

2. What do the supplied figures describe?

Answer and explanation

B. Last year's revenue and operating profit

The figures are historical business results, not targets, market estimates, or transaction terms.

3. Which action is not authorized by the brief?

Answer and explanation

A. Treating an acquisition and 20% revenue target as approved

The case explicitly says no such target or acquisition has been authorized.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Revenue and operating profit are different measures. The historical figures imply a 10% operating margin on the stated basis, but do not tell the team which outcome to prioritize. A growth label should not silently become a revenue target, acquisition mandate, or permission to spend.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
strategic mandate
The authorized purpose and boundaries of a strategy assignment.clarify the strategic mandate
problem statement
A precise description of the issue to be addressed.sharpen the problem statement
decision question
The choice the analysis is intended to support.frame the decision question
executive sponsor
The senior person accountable for backing and directing an initiative.confirm the executive sponsor
objective
The outcome an effort is intended to achieve.define the strategic objective
target
A specified desired level of performance or outcome.set a measurable target
baseline
The starting reference against which a change is assessed.establish the baseline
time horizon
The period over which a decision or outcome is evaluated.agree the time horizon
scope boundary
A limit on what the assignment includes.document the scope boundary
constraint
A condition restricting feasible choices.identify binding constraints
diagnosis
An evidence-based explanation of the central problem or challenge.develop the strategic diagnosis
symptom
An observed sign that may have more than one underlying cause.distinguish a symptom from a cause
hypothesis
A proposition requiring testing against evidence.test the working hypothesis
issue tree
A structured breakdown of a problem into questions.build an issue tree
driver analysis
Examination of factors contributing to an observed result.conduct driver analysis
evidence gap
Missing information needed to support a conclusion.identify an evidence gap
assumption register
A record of premises, evidence status, and owners.maintain the assumption register
fact base
The verified information supporting an analysis.build the fact base
stakeholder map
A description of relevant parties and their interests or roles.prepare a stakeholder map
alignment
Shared understanding of the relevant goal or decision.confirm alignment on the objective
decision rights
The authority to make or approve specified choices.clarify decision rights
success criterion
A condition used to determine whether the effort meets its goal.agree success criteria
strategic option
A distinct possible course of action.develop strategic options
recommendation
A proposed course of action supported by reasoning.present a qualified recommendation

Diagnosis asks what explains the challenge; an option proposes what to do about it. Starting with an acquisition can lock the analysis into one answer before the decision question is settled. A clear mandate preserves the ability to compare genuinely different courses of action.

C Notice the language

Clarifying the assignment is part of senior judgment

A question about the objective need not sound resistant. Explain how different definitions of success would change the options and evidence required. Keep the request focused enough for the sponsor to answer, rather than returning a long list of questions with no decision structure.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Clarify the request
Which outcome should the growth strategy prioritize?
Use the baseline
Last year revenue was $20 million and operating profit was $2 million.
Separate the measures
Revenue growth and profit improvement can point to different choices.
Ask for the horizon
Over what period should we evaluate the result?
Name the boundary
We have not yet agreed a spending limit or scope.
Avoid a premature solution
Acquisition is an option to assess, not the mandate itself.
Request authority
Who will approve the objective and the final recommendation?
Close with a decision
Let us confirm the mandate before Monday's options discussion.
Test the diagnosis
What evidence explains the gap between current performance and the desired outcome?
Mark an assumption
I will label that premise as unverified until its owner confirms it.
Keep a hypothesis open
We should test the cause before designing the response.
Limit the analysis
Which questions would actually change the decision?
Distinguish a target
A 20% revenue figure has not been approved as the goal.
Preserve alternatives
The initial option set should not assume one route is inevitable.
Summarize the gap
We have a historical baseline, but no agreed target or horizon.
Check understanding
Does this question capture the choice you need the team to support?
6 language and precision notes
Growth in what
A useful follow-up names the metric rather than accepting the broad label.
Objective versus route
Profit improvement is an outcome; acquisition is a possible means.
Last year versus next year
Temporal labels prevent a historical result from becoming an implied forecast.
Could versus should
Could identifies an option; should introduces a recommendation that needs a rationale.
Authorized
Use this only for an actual decision, not a promising idea raised in discussion.
Decision-focused question
Ask for the missing input that changes the analysis, not for detail with no clear purpose.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which question best resolves the sponsor's ambiguous growth request?

Answer and explanation

A. Which outcome, target, and time horizon should the strategy prioritize?

The mandate lacks a selected outcome, target, and horizon. Choosing an acquisition, entry route, or approved forecast first would silently supply decisions the sponsor has not made.

2. What operating margin follows from the supplied historical figures?

Answer and explanation

B. 10%

Operating profit of $2 million divided by revenue of $20 million equals 10%.

3. Which sentence correctly labels an acquisition?

Answer and explanation

A. It is one option to assess after clarifying the mandate.

An acquisition is a possible course of action, not a goal or automatic authorization.

4. Which summary best prepares the next discussion?

Answer and explanation

D. We need an objective, target, horizon, boundaries, and decision owner.

The listed inputs resolve the assignment's actual ambiguities without silently making the sponsor's decisions.

Growth is an ambition, not yet a clear assignment

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Daniel: Executive sponsor / Rina: Strategy lead

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • time horizon
  • objective
  • strategic option
  • strategic mandate
  • assumption register
  • baseline

  1. Daniel
    I want a growth strategy ready for discussion on Monday. The business needs a stronger direction, and I would like the team to move quickly.
  2. Rina
    I can focus the work, but first we need the 1. Does growth mean increasing revenue, improving operating profit, or establishing a position in a new market?
  3. Daniel
    Those are all attractive, but I have not ranked them. Last year we had twenty million dollars in revenue and two million in operating profit.
  4. Rina
    That gives us a historical 2. It does not yet tell us which change matters most, or what trade-offs you would accept to achieve it.
  5. Daniel
    I see the distinction. A plan that adds revenue at a lower margin might look good under one measure and weak under another.
  6. Rina
    Exactly. The 3 changes the comparison. We should not choose the measure after seeing which option produces the most attractive number.
  7. Daniel
    What are the few inputs you need from me now? We cannot spend the whole week defining the brief and arrive on Monday without options.
  8. Rina
    A defined 4, a target, and the important constraints. A focused one-year improvement and a longer market-building effort could require very different evidence and commitments.
  9. Daniel
    We have not agreed a spending limit. I also mentioned acquisition in a previous conversation, but I did not approve a transaction.
  10. Rina
    I will treat acquisition as a 5, not the assignment itself. Otherwise we risk evaluating only how to acquire something instead of whether that route addresses the actual problem.
  11. Daniel
    Some people say weak sales execution is the reason growth has slowed. Others say the offer no longer fits what customers need.
  12. Rina
    Those are competing explanations. We need a 6 supported by evidence, rather than selecting whichever explanation makes an existing project appear necessary.
  13. Daniel
    Can you break that investigation into a few questions for the workshop? I want people to see what information could change the recommendation.
  14. Rina
    I can use an 7 to separate customer demand, the offer, and execution questions. It should structure the work, not become a diagram that pretends we already know the answer.
  15. Daniel
    We will also need to distinguish facts from assumptions. Several figures in early presentations came from estimates that nobody formally checked.
  16. Rina
    I will keep an 8 with the source and owner of each material premise. That lets us identify which uncertainty could change the choice before refining the numbers.
  17. Daniel
    I should confirm the outcome and limits, then the team can compare routes. Who else needs a decision role should be explicit as well.
  18. Rina
    Yes. Clear 9 will prevent a workshop preference from being reported as authorization. We can name the sponsor decisions separately from the analytical work assigned to the team.
  19. Daniel
    Send me a one-page mandate before Monday. Leave the target open for my decision; the twenty-percent figure mentioned earlier was not an agreement.
  20. Rina
    I will mark the open 10 and frame the decision for confirmation. The workshop can then compare options against the same objective instead of debating several different meanings of growth.

Answers and explanations
  1. strategic mandate Turn 2. The mandate defines the assignment's purpose and boundaries; the broad request has not yet selected the desired outcome.
  2. baseline Turn 4. The baseline is the prior result used for comparison, not an approved future target or permission to pursue a particular option.
  3. objective Turn 6. The objective specifies the intended outcome and helps determine which options and trade-offs the analysis should compare.
  4. time horizon Turn 8. The time horizon sets the period for assessing the result; short-term improvement and long-term market building may require different options.
  5. strategic option Turn 10. A strategic option is a possible route for assessment; mentioning it does not authorize a transaction or define the outcome.
  6. diagnosis Turn 12. Diagnosis seeks an evidence-based explanation of the challenge; the two suggested causes have not yet been established.
  7. issue tree Turn 14. An issue tree organizes the key analytical questions so evidence gathering remains connected to the decision.
  8. assumption register Turn 16. An assumption register records premises and their verification status so estimates do not become silent facts in later presentations.
  9. decision rights Turn 18. Decision rights identify who can approve the objective, commitments, and recommendation rather than leaving authority implicit.
  10. success criteria Turn 20. Success criteria define how the effort will be judged; the case has not yet agreed a target, horizon, or priority measure.
Read the complete conversation
  1. Daniel: I want a growth strategy ready for discussion on Monday. The business needs a stronger direction, and I would like the team to move quickly.
  2. Rina: I can focus the work, but first we need the strategic mandate. Does growth mean increasing revenue, improving operating profit, or establishing a position in a new market?
  3. Daniel: Those are all attractive, but I have not ranked them. Last year we had twenty million dollars in revenue and two million in operating profit.
  4. Rina: That gives us a historical baseline. It does not yet tell us which change matters most, or what trade-offs you would accept to achieve it.
  5. Daniel: I see the distinction. A plan that adds revenue at a lower margin might look good under one measure and weak under another.
  6. Rina: Exactly. The objective changes the comparison. We should not choose the measure after seeing which option produces the most attractive number.
  7. Daniel: What are the few inputs you need from me now? We cannot spend the whole week defining the brief and arrive on Monday without options.
  8. Rina: A defined time horizon, a target, and the important constraints. A focused one-year improvement and a longer market-building effort could require very different evidence and commitments.
  9. Daniel: We have not agreed a spending limit. I also mentioned acquisition in a previous conversation, but I did not approve a transaction.
  10. Rina: I will treat acquisition as a strategic option, not the assignment itself. Otherwise we risk evaluating only how to acquire something instead of whether that route addresses the actual problem.
  11. Daniel: Some people say weak sales execution is the reason growth has slowed. Others say the offer no longer fits what customers need.
  12. Rina: Those are competing explanations. We need a diagnosis supported by evidence, rather than selecting whichever explanation makes an existing project appear necessary.
  13. Daniel: Can you break that investigation into a few questions for the workshop? I want people to see what information could change the recommendation.
  14. Rina: I can use an issue tree to separate customer demand, the offer, and execution questions. It should structure the work, not become a diagram that pretends we already know the answer.
  15. Daniel: We will also need to distinguish facts from assumptions. Several figures in early presentations came from estimates that nobody formally checked.
  16. Rina: I will keep an assumption register with the source and owner of each material premise. That lets us identify which uncertainty could change the choice before refining the numbers.
  17. Daniel: I should confirm the outcome and limits, then the team can compare routes. Who else needs a decision role should be explicit as well.
  18. Rina: Yes. Clear decision rights will prevent a workshop preference from being reported as authorization. We can name the sponsor decisions separately from the analytical work assigned to the team.
  19. Daniel: Send me a one-page mandate before Monday. Leave the target open for my decision; the twenty-percent figure mentioned earlier was not an agreement.
  20. Rina: I will mark the open success criteria and frame the decision for confirmation. The workshop can then compare options against the same objective instead of debating several different meanings of growth.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Which growth problem are we solving?

The lesson's executive requests a growth strategy without specifying revenue, profit, or market entry as the priority.

  1. Strategy lead: When you ask for a growth strategy, is the priority revenue, profit, or entry into another market?
  2. Executive sponsor: I haven't chosen among those. I was assuming the same strategy would deliver all three.
  3. Strategy lead: They may involve different choices. Could we clarify the ambition before building a strategic thesis?
  4. Executive sponsor: What would a precise diagnosis add beyond a list of attractive growth initiatives?
  5. Strategy lead: It identifies the problem we're trying to solve, rather than assuming every opportunity addresses it.
  6. Executive sponsor: Then our issue tree should separate those three possible objectives instead of merge them.
  7. Strategy lead: Exactly. We can ask what evidence would make each objective a priority and what constraints apply.
  8. Executive sponsor: Please bring those questions into the discussion without inventing a target or investment budget.
  9. Strategy lead: I will. The immediate output is a clarified decision question, not a fully approved growth direction.
  10. Executive sponsor: Good. Let's establish the objective before requesting initiatives that might answer the wrong question.
Retention or acquisition behind the revenue concern

Separate fictional strategy diagnosis: customer acquisition is unchanged, repeat purchases have fallen, and leadership asks for more advertising. Causes are unconfirmed.

  1. Commercial director: Revenue needs attention. Could you build a strategy around increasing advertising immediately?
  2. Strategy analyst: Before selecting a response, can we clarify the problem? Acquisition is unchanged, while repeat purchases have fallen.
  3. Commercial director: So our diagnosis should examine retention rather than assume new-customer volume caused the weakness.
  4. Strategy analyst: It should investigate repeat purchasing, yes, without claiming we already know why it declined.
  5. Commercial director: Could the issue tree separate purchase frequency, customer loss, and changes in order value?
  6. Strategy analyst: Yes. Those are questions to test, not confirmed causes supplied by the current figures.
  7. Commercial director: What would you ask me to clarify about the ambition for this work?
  8. Strategy analyst: Whether we are prioritizing restored repeat revenue, total revenue growth, or profitability, and over what horizon.
  9. Commercial director: I'll define that objective before treating additional advertising as the strategic thesis.
  10. Strategy analyst: Then we can assess interventions against the actual diagnosis rather than start with a favored solution.
A capacity symptom needs a bounded question

Separate fictional strategy exercise: one service team has a six-week backlog, while capacity elsewhere in the company has not been assessed.

  1. Chief operating officer: One team has a six-week backlog. Should our strategy be to acquire another service company?
  2. Strategy director: Could we first clarify whether the priority is reducing that backlog or expanding long-term capability?
  3. Chief operating officer: I was treating them as the same problem, but the immediate concern is waiting work.
  4. Strategy director: Then our diagnosis should examine demand, capacity, and work flow before selecting an acquisition response.
  5. Chief operating officer: Do we know whether another internal team has spare capacity that could help?
  6. Strategy director: No. Capacity elsewhere hasn't been assessed, so we shouldn't assume either spare resources or universal shortage.
  7. Chief operating officer: Let's frame the issue around the affected service and the six-week backlog first.
  8. Strategy director: Agreed. An issue tree can organize the questions without making the proposed acquisition the answer in advance.
  9. Chief operating officer: I'll clarify the desired service outcome and any constraints for that investigation.
  10. Strategy director: Then we'll assess strategic options after the problem and evidence are properly defined.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Growth is an ambition, not yet a clear assignment
  1. Check the cloze key, then read the sponsor discussion. State $20 million revenue and $2 million operating profit as last year's baseline, not next year's targets.
  2. Switch roles for the mandate questions. Preserve the unresolved objective, horizon, scope, spending limit, and decision rights instead of inventing answers.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A market-entry label hides the outcome

A sponsor proposes opening an overseas office but has not stated the intended business outcome or budget. The team has no authority to sign a lease.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Analyst: "An overseas office is a possible ___."

Answer and explanation

A. option

Opening an office is a course of action, not the business outcome it is intended to produce.

2. Sponsor: "We first need to define the ___."

Answer and explanation

B. objective

The intended business outcome remains unstated, so it must be clarified before evaluating the option.

3. Analyst: "The spending limit remains ___."

Answer and explanation

D. unagreed

The briefing supplies no agreed budget, so a spending amount must not be invented.

4. Sponsor: "This discussion does not authorize a ___."

Answer and explanation

C. lease

The team expressly lacks authority to sign a lease for the proposed office.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.

Lesson 01: Strategy Role, Problem Framing, and Executive Diagnosis
Original fictional case: Executive sponsor Daniel asks strategy lead Rina for a growth strategy. Last year the business reported $20 million revenue and $2 million operating profit. The sponsor has not chosen whether the primary objective is revenue growth, operating-profit improvement, or entry into a new market. No target, horizon, or spending limit has been agreed. A workshop is scheduled for Monday. Rina must establish the decision question and missing inputs rather than assume that an acquisition or a 20% revenue target has already been authorized.
Language workshop: Growth is an ambition, not yet a clear assignment
Communication goal: Clarify an executive mandate before selecting a growth option or commissioning broad analysis.
Language guidance: Revenue and operating profit are different measures. The historical figures imply a 10% operating margin on the stated basis, but do not tell the team which outcome to prioritize. A growth label should not silently become a revenue target, acquisition mandate, or permission to spend.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Which outcome should the growth strategy prioritize? / Last year revenue was $20 million and operating profit was $2 million. / Revenue growth and profit improvement can point to different choices. / Over what period should we evaluate the result? / We have not yet agreed a spending limit or scope. / Acquisition is an option to assess, not the mandate itself. / Who will approve the objective and the final recommendation? / Let us confirm the mandate before Monday's options discussion. / What evidence explains the gap between current performance and the desired outcome? / I will label that premise as unverified until its owner confirms it. / We should test the cause before designing the response. / Which questions would actually change the decision? / A 20% revenue figure has not been approved as the goal. / The initial option set should not assume one route is inevitable. / We have a historical baseline, but no agreed target or horizon. / Does this question capture the choice you need the team to support?

Switch roles for the mandate questions. Preserve the unresolved objective, horizon, scope, spending limit, and decision rights instead of inventing answers. TASK: Choose grammar that preserves the meaning
1. Use the lesson's language workshop, or one actual sentence from the dialogue, to explain a single grammar distinction in no more than 90 words. Show how it affects timing, certainty, responsibility or politeness.
2. Give one brief occupational exchange containing a gap and four complete options A-D. Supply enough context for exactly one answer. Keep distractors plausible; distinguish grammar errors from wording that changes the facts. Stop and wait.

4. Repeat with three new exchanges, one at a time, moving from recognition to a more subtle meaning contrast. Do not copy the published checks. Label invented variations and do not turn uncertainty into a promise.
5. End with a short contrast table and two supported spoken turns using supplied frames. Accept accurate alternatives in oral practice; acknowledge and replace ambiguous multiple-choice items.

Scope: Original fictional language practice, not investment, legal, accounting, valuation, or transaction advice. Figures are teaching assumptions, not forecasts. Lesson 01: Strategy Role, Problem Framing, and Executive Diagnosis
Original fictional case: Executive sponsor Daniel asks strategy lead Rina for a growth strategy. Last year the business reported $20 million revenue and $2 million operating profit. The sponsor has not chosen whether the primary objective is revenue growth, operating-profit improvement, or entry into a new market. No target, horizon, or spending limit has been agreed. A workshop is scheduled for Monday. Rina must establish the decision question and missing inputs rather than assume that an acquisition or a 20% revenue target has already been authorized.
Language workshop: Growth is an ambition, not yet a clear assignment
Communication goal: Clarify an executive mandate before selecting a growth option or commissioning broad analysis.
Language guidance: Revenue and operating profit are different measures. The historical figures imply a 10% operating margin on the stated basis, but do not tell the team which outcome to prioritize. A growth label should not silently become a revenue target, acquisition mandate, or permission to spend.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Which outcome should the growth strategy prioritize? / Last year revenue was $20 million and operating profit was $2 million. / Revenue growth and profit improvement can point to different choices. / Over what period should we evaluate the result? / We have not yet agreed a spending limit or scope. / Acquisition is an option to assess, not the mandate itself. / Who will approve the objective and the final recommendation? / Let us confirm the mandate before Monday's options discussion. / What evidence explains the gap between current performance and the desired outcome? / I will label that premise as unverified until its owner confirms it. / We should test the cause before designing the response. / Which questions would actually change the decision? / A 20% revenue figure has not been approved as the goal. / The initial option set should not assume one route is inevitable. / We have a historical baseline, but no agreed target or horizon. / Does this question capture the choice you need the team to support?
Vocabulary: strategic mandate: The authorized purpose and boundaries of a strategy assignment. / problem statement: A precise description of the issue to be addressed. / decision question: The choice the analysis is intended to support. / executive sponsor: The senior person accountable for backing and directing an initiative. / objective: The outcome an effort is intended to achieve. / target: A specified desired level of performance or outcome. / baseline: The starting reference against which a change is assessed. / time horizon: The period over which a decision or outcome is evaluated. / scope boundary: A limit on what the assignment includes. / constraint: A condition restricting feasible choices. / diagnosis: An evidence-based explanation of the central problem or challenge. / symptom: An observed sign that may have more than one underlying cause. / hypothesis: A proposition requiring testing against evidence. / issue tree: A structured breakdown of a problem into questions. / driver analysis: Examination of factors contributing to an observed result. / evidence gap: Missing information needed to support a conclusion. / assumption register: A record of premises, evidence status, and owners. / fact base: The verified information supporting an analysis. / stakeholder map: A description of relevant parties and their interests or roles. / alignment: Shared understanding of the relevant goal or decision. / decision rights: The authority to make or approve specified choices. / success criterion: A condition used to determine whether the effort meets its goal. / strategic option: A distinct possible course of action. / recommendation: A proposed course of action supported by reasoning.
Speaking task: Check the cloze key, then read the sponsor discussion. State $20 million revenue and $2 million operating profit as last year's baseline, not next year's targets. Switch roles for the mandate questions. Preserve the unresolved objective, horizon, scope, spending limit, and decision rights instead of inventing answers. Complete and check the overseas-office exchange. Contrast an option with an objective, and retain the absence of lease authority.
Partner: Daniel: Executive sponsor / Rina: Strategy lead
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A sponsor proposes opening an overseas office but has not stated the intended business outcome or budget. The team has no authority to sign a lease.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Daniel: I should confirm the outcome and limits, then the team can compare routes. Who else needs a decision role should be explicit as well.
Rina: Yes. Clear decision rights will prevent a workshop preference from being reported as authorization. We can name the sponsor decisions separately from the analytical work assigned to the team.
Daniel: Send me a one-page mandate before Monday. Leave the target open for my decision; the twenty-percent figure mentioned earlier was not an agreement.
Rina: I will mark the open success criteria and frame the decision for confirmation. The workshop can then compare options against the same objective instead of debating several different meanings of growth.
END REFERENCE

02Strategic Choices: Ambition, Where to Play, How to Win, and TradeoffsTwo priorities competing for the same specialist team+

Your goal

Make a strategic trade-off explicit when two attractive initiatives cannot both fit the available capacity.

This lesson in the book, page 13 ↗

A Read the situation

Two priorities competing for the same specialist team

For the next quarter, a service business has 160 specialist-weeks available after existing commitments. Improving the core service requires 120 specialist-weeks; entering an adjacent segment requires 100. Both need the same specialists. A draft strategy says to deliver both in full next quarter without explaining the 60-week shortfall. No additional hiring, outsourcing, or reduced scope has been approved. Strategy manager Sana and business-unit head Victor must compare choices and sequencing without treating ambition as extra capacity.

Sana: Strategy manager / Victor: Business-unit head

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. How much capacity do both full initiatives require?

Answer and explanation

D. 220 specialist-weeks

The two requirements are 120 and 100 specialist-weeks, totaling 220.

2. What is the shortfall against available capacity?

Answer and explanation

D. 60 specialist-weeks

Required capacity of 220 minus available capacity of 160 leaves a 60-week gap.

3. Which assumption is unsupported?

Answer and explanation

C. Extra staffing or reduced scope has already been approved.

The briefing explicitly says hiring, outsourcing, and scope reductions have not been approved.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

The resource gap is 60 specialist-weeks, not 60 people and not automatically a cash budget of any particular size. Available capacity already excludes existing commitments. Do not count the same specialist time twice or treat an unapproved recruitment idea as immediately usable capacity.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
strategic ambition
The overall level or direction of desired achievement.articulate the strategic ambition
where to play
The markets, customers, or activities selected for competition.define where to play
how to win
The proposed basis for succeeding in the chosen arena.explain how to win
trade-off
A choice that sacrifices one benefit to obtain another.make the trade-off explicit
opportunity cost
The value of the next-best alternative forgone.assess opportunity cost
capacity constraint
A limit imposed by the amount of usable resources.quantify the capacity constraint
resource envelope
The total resources available within defined boundaries.work within the resource envelope
core business
The established activities central to the company's current operation.strengthen the core business
adjacency
A related market or activity beyond the current core.evaluate an adjacency
strategic focus
Concentration on a selected set of choices and priorities.maintain strategic focus
differentiation
A relevant distinction that gives customers a reason to choose an offering.substantiate differentiation
cost advantage
A relative cost position that can support competitive performance.test the cost advantage
competitive positioning
The chosen place and proposition relative to alternatives.clarify competitive positioning
activity system
A set of mutually supporting activities that deliver a strategy.align the activity system
strategic fit
Compatibility among choices, capabilities, and the intended direction.assess strategic fit
operational effectiveness
Performing activities well relative to their required standard or alternatives.improve operational effectiveness
cannibalization
A new offering reducing demand or revenue for the company's existing offering.estimate cannibalization
sequencing
Ordering initiatives over time according to priorities and dependencies.agree the sequencing
phased rollout
Introduction through defined stages rather than all at once.propose a phased rollout
minimum viable scope
The smallest scope sufficient for the specified purpose or learning goal.define minimum viable scope
deprioritization
A decision to give an activity less priority or delay it.document deprioritization
stop-doing list
An explicit set of activities to discontinue or suspend.maintain a stop-doing list
resource bottleneck
A resource whose limited availability restricts overall progress.identify the resource bottleneck
commitment
An agreed allocation or obligation rather than a tentative proposal.distinguish a commitment from an option

Doing both may be feasible only with a changed sequence, scope, or resource plan. Those are options to evaluate, not facts that repair the current plan. The strategic choice also needs the relative value and evidence for each route, not just the fact that one requires fewer weeks.

C Notice the language

Make the conflict visible before asking for a choice

A leader may call two initiatives priorities because both have merit. Respect that ambition while showing the shared resource they consume. A useful challenge quantifies the conflict, names the alternatives, and distinguishes an authorized commitment from a proposal for more capacity.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Respect the ambition
Both initiatives may have value, but the current plan does not fit.
Show the arithmetic
The two initiatives require 220 specialist-weeks against 160 available.
Name the gap
We are short by 60 specialist-weeks.
Identify the shared resource
Both proposals depend on the same specialist team.
Request the choice
Which outcome takes priority if we cannot deliver both in full?
Offer alternatives
We can compare sequencing, reduced scope, or a properly approved capacity plan.
Avoid invented resources
No extra hiring or outsourcing has been approved.
Close with a commitment
The final plan must name what happens now and what waits.
Test the arena
Which segment are we choosing to serve first?
Explain the advantage
Why would customers choose us in that segment?
Preserve the distinction
Operational improvement and a new market position are not identical choices.
Name the sacrifice
Funding this route means delaying or reducing another use of the team.
Check the ramp
New staff would need realistic onboarding and availability assumptions.
Limit a pilot
A smaller scope should answer a defined question.
Record the non-choice
The strategy should state what we are not committing to this quarter.
Confirm the units
These figures are specialist-weeks, not headcount.
6 language and precision notes
Both are priorities
The statement does not resolve an actual competition for shared resources.
Now versus later
Sequencing can change timing without pretending that every initiative fits today.
Requires versus has
Separate the resource demand from the capacity already available.
Could add capacity
This introduces a proposal and its dependencies, not an existing resource.
Foregone alternative
Name the specific next-best use when explaining opportunity cost.
Full scope
Keep this qualifier when a smaller pilot might fit but the original commitments do not.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which statement reports the constraint precisely?

Answer and explanation

A. Full delivery needs 220 specialist-weeks, exceeding current capacity by 60.

Combined demand, not each separate request, must be compared with the available specialist-weeks.

2. Which proposal is correctly described as an option?

Answer and explanation

B. Evaluate a phased approach without claiming it is already approved.

A phased approach is a possible plan to assess, while the other options conceal or invent capacity.

3. Which question addresses how to win rather than where to play?

Answer and explanation

B. Why would the selected customers prefer our offer to their current alternatives?

Customer preference and the basis of advantage address how to win. Selecting segments, geography, and categories defines the arena, or where to play.

4. Which conclusion follows from the resource data alone?

Answer and explanation

A. Both full initiatives cannot fit the stated capacity without a change.

Capacity establishes feasibility limits but does not alone rank the options' value or prove their profitability.

Check explanations in the book, page 87 ↗

E Conversations

Two priorities competing for the same specialist team

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Sana: Strategy manager / Victor: Business-unit head

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

  • stop-doing list
  • resource envelope

  • where to play
  1. Victor
    Keep both initiatives in next quarter's plan. The core service needs attention, but I do not want the adjacent launch slipping again.
  2. Sana
    Then we need a decision about the 1. We have one hundred sixty specialist-weeks after existing commitments; the full proposals need two hundred twenty.
  3. Victor

  4. Sana

  5. Victor

  6. Sana

  7. Victor

  8. Sana

  9. Victor

  10. Sana

  11. Victor

  12. Sana

  13. Victor

  14. Sana
    We can define a 7 around a specific learning question and estimate the work. We cannot assume forty weeks is enough without that design.
  15. Victor

  16. Sana
    Agreed. Compare the resource plan with 8, including what starts next quarter and what waits. Neither option is already authorized.
  17. Victor

Answers and explanations
  1. capacity constraint Turn 2. The capacity constraint is the limited 160 specialist-weeks shared by both initiatives, not a judgment that either lacks value.
  2. resource bottleneck Turn 4. The resource bottleneck arises because both initiatives need the same limited specialist team; separate sponsorship does not create separate capacity.
  3. resource envelope Turn 6. The resource envelope is the bounded amount actually available; efficiency hopes do not establish additional usable resources.
  4. where to play Turn 8. Where to play identifies the arena selected for competition, such as the current core or the adjacent segment.
  5. how to win Turn 10. How to win concerns the proposed basis of success with the selected customers, which market size alone does not establish.
  6. opportunity cost Turn 12. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone, including the delayed use of scarce specialist time.
  7. minimum viable scope Turn 14. Minimum viable scope must be sufficient for the specified purpose or learning question; merely shrinking work does not make a useful pilot.
  8. sequencing Turn 16. Sequencing orders initiatives over time and can address shared-resource conflicts without assuming immediate new staffing.
  9. stop-doing list Turn 18. A stop-doing list makes discontinued or suspended work explicit, preventing new priorities from simply accumulating on top of existing demand.
  10. commitment Turn 20. A commitment is the chosen, authorized plan with resources and limits; it differs from the unapproved alternatives discussed in the meeting.
Read the complete conversation
  1. Victor: Keep both initiatives in next quarter's plan. The core service needs attention, but I do not want the adjacent launch slipping again.
  2. Sana: Then we need a decision about the capacity constraint. We have one hundred sixty specialist-weeks after existing commitments; the full proposals need two hundred twenty.
  3. Victor: Each request was below one hundred sixty when I reviewed it. Why are we only raising this now?

  8. Sana: Start with where to play: strengthen the core or enter the adjacent segment first. Neither label tells us which choice creates more value.
  9. Victor: The adjacent proposal has a large market estimate. Its customer argument is thinner; we have not shown why buyers would switch.
  10. Sana: That is the how to win question. We need a reason customers prefer our service, supported by capabilities and evidence, before size becomes an entry recommendation.
  11. Victor: The core work uses one hundred twenty weeks. Choosing it first leaves forty, but it also delays the other opportunity.
  12. Sana: Yes. Compare that opportunity cost explicitly. Forty remaining weeks would not deliver a hundred-week launch, and unused capacity is not the only consideration.
  13. Victor: Could forty weeks fund a useful test of the adjacent offer? I am asking about feasibility, not approving a smaller project.
  14. Sana: We can define a minimum viable scope around a specific learning question and estimate the work. We cannot assume forty weeks is enough without that design.
  15. Victor: Put that beside hiring. New people will need approval and onboarding; they will not appear fully productive next Monday.
  16. Sana: Agreed. Compare the resource plan with sequencing, including what starts next quarter and what waits. Neither option is already authorized.
  17. Victor: I also want a page showing what stops. Otherwise another priority will arrive and we will have this argument again.
  18. Sana: I will include a stop-doing list with the consequences of each choice. Removing work needs a decision too; it cannot remain an unnamed assumption.

Dialogue in the book, page 19 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Core improvement and market entry share the same people

The lesson's team can invest in its core service or enter a new segment; staff capacity is limited and shared.

  1. Strategy manager: Both options use the same limited staff. We can't compare them as if each had a separate team.
  2. Business sponsor: Could we call both priorities and ask people to deliver them alongside normal work?
  3. Strategy manager: That avoids the tradeoff rather than resolves it. The opportunity cost is what those people cannot do instead.
  4. Business sponsor: The core-service option strengthens existing work, whereas segment entry pursues a new customer group.
  5. Strategy manager: Yes. We should compare the same staffing period, expected outcomes, and uncertainty for both.
  6. Business sponsor: We haven't quantified those outcomes, so neither option has a proven higher return yet.
  7. Strategy manager: Correct. The activity system also matters: which supporting work each choice would require.
  8. Business sponsor: I'll ask both proposal owners to identify displaced work instead of hiding the resource conflict.
  9. Strategy manager: Then we can present a real strategic choice with common criteria and its weaker side visible.
  10. Business sponsor: Good. Our next discussion will prioritize, not simply add two labels to an overloaded team.
A focused pilot or a wider launch

Separate fictional strategy exercise: with the same six-person team for a quarter, option A serves one segment and includes research; B serves three segments but has no research capacity.

  1. Growth director: Option B reaches three segments, so it looks stronger than the one-segment pilot.
  2. Strategy analyst: Both use six people for the quarter, but only A includes capacity for customer research.
  3. Growth director: Then the tradeoff is broader initial coverage versus more deliberate learning in one segment.
  4. Strategy analyst: Exactly. More segments doesn't itself prove more profitable growth, especially with their needs still untested.
  5. Growth director: Could we keep B's reach and add A's research without changing the team?
  6. Strategy analyst: Not under these supplied options. We'd need to reassess scope rather than assume extra capacity.
  7. Growth director: I favor learning first, but want the lost early coverage stated as the opportunity cost.
  8. Strategy analyst: I'll make that explicit and retain the same quarterly staffing basis for the comparison.
  9. Growth director: Then the recommendation can explain a strategic choice instead of calling one option best at everything.
  10. Strategy analyst: Agreed. We can propose A for review while keeping its narrower reach visible.
Customization versus a repeatable service

Separate fictional strategy workshop: option A offers bespoke implementations with more configuration work; B standardizes the service but excludes some requested custom features. Revenue effects are unknown.

  1. Product director: The bespoke option answers more individual requests. Should we call it the obvious way to win?
  2. Operations strategist: It also requires more configuration work, whereas the standardized option excludes some custom features.
  3. Product director: So we should compare customer fit and delivery effort rather than count features alone.
  4. Operations strategist: Yes. Those choices imply different activity systems, not just different descriptions of the same offer.
  5. Product director: Do we know whether broader customization produces enough revenue to justify that work?
  6. Operations strategist: No. Revenue effects are unknown here, so neither margin advantage is established.
  7. Product director: I'll describe the opportunity cost of standardization as requests we deliberately don't support.
  8. Operations strategist: And describe the bespoke option's tradeoff as additional configuration work rather than free flexibility.
  9. Product director: Let's assess both over the same customer scope and planning horizon before recommending one.
  10. Operations strategist: Good. A useful strategic choice states what we give up as clearly as what we pursue.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Two priorities competing for the same specialist team
  1. After checking the answers, read Victor and Sana's exchange. Stress combined demand: 120 plus 100 is 220 specialist-weeks against 160 available.
  2. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Keep the forty-week pilot as an option requiring design, not an approved substitute for the full launch.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

Two pilots still share one team

A team has 90 analyst-days available. Pilot A needs 55 days and Pilot B needs 50. No additional capacity or scope reduction has been approved.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Lead: "The combined requirement is ___ analyst-days."

Answer and explanation

B. 105

Adding the two pilot requirements gives 55 plus 50, or 105 analyst-days.

2. Analyst: "That exceeds available capacity by ___ days."

Answer and explanation

C. 15

The shortfall is 105 required minus 90 available, which equals 15 analyst-days.

3. Lead: "We need an explicit resource or sequencing ___."

Answer and explanation

C. choice

The current full-scope combination cannot fit without changing resources, timing, or scope through a decision.

4. Analyst: "Neither proposal creates extra ___ by itself."

Answer and explanation

B. capacity

A proposed initiative adds demand, not usable analyst time or approval for additional resources.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Original fictional case: For the next quarter, a service business has 160 specialist-weeks available after existing commitments. Improving the core service requires 120 specialist-weeks; entering an adjacent segment requires 100. Both need the same specialists. A draft strategy says to deliver both in full next quarter without explaining the 60-week shortfall. No additional hiring, outsourcing, or reduced scope has been approved. Strategy manager Sana and business-unit head Victor must compare choices and sequencing without treating ambition as extra capacity.
Language workshop: Two priorities competing for the same specialist team
Communication goal: Make a strategic trade-off explicit when two attractive initiatives cannot both fit the available capacity.
Language guidance: The resource gap is 60 specialist-weeks, not 60 people and not automatically a cash budget of any particular size. Available capacity already excludes existing commitments. Do not count the same specialist time twice or treat an unapproved recruitment idea as immediately usable capacity.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Both initiatives may have value, but the current plan does not fit. / The two initiatives require 220 specialist-weeks against 160 available. / We are short by 60 specialist-weeks. / Both proposals depend on the same specialist team. / Which outcome takes priority if we cannot deliver both in full? / We can compare sequencing, reduced scope, or a properly approved capacity plan. / No extra hiring or outsourcing has been approved. / The final plan must name what happens now and what waits. / Which segment are we choosing to serve first? / Why would customers choose us in that segment? / Operational improvement and a new market position are not identical choices. / Funding this route means delaying or reducing another use of the team. / New staff would need realistic onboarding and availability assumptions. / A smaller scope should answer a defined question. / The strategy should state what we are not committing to this quarter. / These figures are specialist-weeks, not headcount.
Vocabulary: strategic ambition: The overall level or direction of desired achievement. / where to play: The markets, customers, or activities selected for competition. / how to win: The proposed basis for succeeding in the chosen arena. / trade-off: A choice that sacrifices one benefit to obtain another. / opportunity cost: The value of the next-best alternative forgone. / capacity constraint: A limit imposed by the amount of usable resources. / resource envelope: The total resources available within defined boundaries. / core business: The established activities central to the company's current operation. / adjacency: A related market or activity beyond the current core. / strategic focus: Concentration on a selected set of choices and priorities. / differentiation: A relevant distinction that gives customers a reason to choose an offering. / cost advantage: A relative cost position that can support competitive performance. / competitive positioning: The chosen place and proposition relative to alternatives. / activity system: A set of mutually supporting activities that deliver a strategy. / strategic fit: Compatibility among choices, capabilities, and the intended direction. / operational effectiveness: Performing activities well relative to their required standard or alternatives. / cannibalization: A new offering reducing demand or revenue for the company's existing offering. / sequencing: Ordering initiatives over time according to priorities and dependencies. / phased rollout: Introduction through defined stages rather than all at once. / minimum viable scope: The smallest scope sufficient for the specified purpose or learning goal. / deprioritization: A decision to give an activity less priority or delay it. / stop-doing list: An explicit set of activities to discontinue or suspend. / resource bottleneck: A resource whose limited availability restricts overall progress. / commitment: An agreed allocation or obligation rather than a tentative proposal.
Speaking task: After checking the answers, read Victor and Sana's exchange. Stress combined demand: 120 plus 100 is 220 specialist-weeks against 160 available. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Keep the forty-week pilot as an option requiring design, not an approved substitute for the full launch. Complete the two-pilot exchange and check the key. Read 105 required, 90 available, and 15 short clearly, retaining analyst-days as the unit.

Victor: Bring the customer evidence, expected value, and feasible scopes to the meeting. Leave the full-delivery promise out until we choose.
Sana: Then we can record a deliverable commitment: one resource plan, named priorities, and explicit timing. The sixty-week gap stays visible until a decision resolves it.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
